headline_en: Coordinated effort needed to rehabilitate workers returning from abroad
summary_en: Report of a roundtable on safe migration and reintegration of returnees held on Tuesday 18 August 2026 at the Prothom Alo office in Karwan Bazar, Dhaka, jointly organised by BRAC Migration Programme and Prothom Alo with European Union support. Expatriates' welfare minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the whole process of sending workers abroad is to be moved online, a 'Probashi Card' is to be finalised under the government's 180-day programme, and employer representatives now verify workers' skills, as with 6,000 drivers for the UAE. Officials from passport, airport police, civil aviation, Wage Earners' Welfare Board, NSDA, BAIRA, ILO, banks and SME bodies spoke about fraud, fake documents, returnees' lack of savings and financing.

facts.statement: A roundtable titled 'Safe migration and reintegration of returnees: reality and what to do' was held on Tuesday 18 August 2026 at the Prothom Alo office, Karwan Bazar, Dhaka, jointly organised by BRAC Migration Programme and Prothom Alo with the support of the European Union.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said an initiative is being taken to make the entire process of sending workers abroad from Bangladesh online, and that information management on recruiting agencies' validity (legality) and on worker demand from abroad will be made more transparent.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury

facts.statement: The expatriates' welfare minister said an initiative is under way to identify and act against the rings involved in sending people abroad by illegal routes, and that a mass awareness campaign is planned for the coming one month in several districts, starting from Sunamganj-Habiganj and including Madaripur.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury

facts.statement: The minister said that foreign employers often do not get workers with the skill they asked for, causing problems for both worker and employer; so when a country asks for workers of a specific skill, a system has been introduced for that country's employer representatives to verify (test) them. This process is being followed in taking 6,000 drivers from Bangladesh to the United Arab Emirates.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury

facts.statement: As of August 2026 a recruitment of 6,000 drivers from Bangladesh to the United Arab Emirates was in progress, with employer representatives verifying the candidates' skills.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury

facts.statement: The minister said the government plans to launch a 'Probashi Card' (expatriate card) for migrants and that the card will be finalised as part of the government's 180-day programme.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury

facts.statement: The minister listed other plans: quickly preparing madrasa students, who are already ahead in Arabic, for the Middle East labour market; involving Bangladesh's private-sector institutions in sending skilled manpower abroad; finding new labour markets; helping returnees go back to their previous occupation; and bringing home the bodies of migrants who die abroad as well as assisting their families.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury

facts.statement: BRAC's concept paper, presented by BRAC Associate Director (Migration) Shariful Islam Hasan, said returnees' big problems are having no savings, getting no chance to use skills gained abroad, and being unable to restart a livelihood at home. For safe migration it stressed district and upazila level awareness work, training, language teaching, involving police and religious leaders, and countering traffickers' publicity on social media.
facts.source_in_article: Shariful Islam Hasan, BRAC (concept paper)

facts.statement: European Union programme manager in Dhaka Nurul Quader said migration should be seen as a business model with the interests and responsibilities of government, banks, recruiting agencies and all parties made clear, and that people's mindset and awareness must be addressed to stop the tendency to go abroad after being cheated and spending huge sums.
facts.source_in_article: Nurul Quader, EU programme manager, Dhaka

facts.statement: Airport Armed Police Battalion DIG (Operations) Md. Al-Mamunul Ansari said that the risk of irregularities has increased since police verification was abolished for issuing passports, and that coordination is needed among the airport, passport and 'police clearance' systems to ensure safe migration.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Al-Mamunul Ansari, DIG (Operations), Airport Armed Police Battalion

facts.statement: A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, joint secretary of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board and director of the RAISE project, said a large part of the problems could be reduced if women workers were sent through training and the regular process, and that if protection is not ensured at departure the problem of rehabilitating returnees will continue.
facts.source_in_article: A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, Wage Earners' Welfare Board / RAISE project

facts.statement: Ali Haider Chowdhury, former secretary general of the Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies (BAIRA), said government and the private sector must jointly make an integrated policy to stop irregularities in the migration sector and everyone involved must be made accountable.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Haider Chowdhury, former BAIRA secretary general

facts.statement: Jahangir Hossain, Director (Skills Standards and Curriculum) of the National Skills Development Authority (NSDA), said training is being given to develop returnee workers as entrepreneurs.
facts.source_in_article: Jahangir Hossain, NSDA

facts.statement: Squadron Leader Rakib Ahmed Tawab, Deputy Director (QA and I) of the Civil Aviation Authority, said checks are being carried out at the airport to stop attempts to go abroad with fake visas, fake documents and fake BMET cards, and that many returnees come back mentally shattered, which is a big challenge for airport authorities to handle.
facts.source_in_article: Rakib Ahmed Tawab, Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh

facts.statement: ILO National Programme Officer Mahsin Hamuda advised coordinating government and private-sector work on returnees and making it easier for returnees to become entrepreneurs.
facts.source_in_article: Mahsin Hamuda, ILO

facts.statement: BAIRA joint secretary and administrator Md. Badrul Haque said that to ensure safe migration the rings of brokers and irregularities must be brought under control down to village level and legal action taken against them. (The article identifies him as BAIRA's 'administrator'.)
facts.source_in_article: Md. Badrul Haque, BAIRA

facts.statement: SME Foundation managing director Anwar Hossain Chowdhury said many who return after long work abroad face mental stress, a jobs crisis and inability to join the mainstream; Bangladesh Krishi Bank general manager Md. Mostafizur Rahman said financing for returnees' rehabilitation and business start-up must be made easier.
facts.source_in_article: Anwar Hossain Chowdhury (SME Foundation); Md. Mostafizur Rahman (Bangladesh Krishi Bank)

facts.statement: Mahmudur Rifat Khan, executive officer of the National Association of Small and Cottage Industries of Bangladesh, said coordination among ministries and stakeholders must increase and policy decisions on safe migration and returnee rehabilitation must actually be implemented.
facts.source_in_article: Mahmudur Rifat Khan

facts.statement: A T M Abu Asad, Additional Director General of the Department of Immigration and Passports, acknowledged there are complaints of harassment and extra spending in passport renewal, and said that because of the old tendency to take passports with false information or multiple identities, embassies abroad have become concerned about the information in Bangladeshi passports.
facts.source_in_article: A T M Abu Asad, Department of Immigration and Passports

facts.statement: Libya returnees Hridoy Chowdhury and Mahbubur Rahman and Tofayel Ahmed, who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, described their experiences at the roundtable (the article gives no details of their accounts). Probashi Kallyan Bank deputy managing director Md. Jahangir Hossain also spoke.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

headline_en: Why demand for Bangladeshi workers is falling in Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Oman
summary_en: A June 2025 report on the narrowing of Bangladesh's overseas labour markets. Saudi Arabia took 73% of workers leaving in January-May 2025 but paused visas in June 2025, while the UAE, Oman (since 2024) and Malaysia (since June 2024) were closed. It gives BMET figures on total and female departures for 2022 to May 2025 and explains why women's migration is falling.

facts.statement: Of all Bangladeshi workers who have ever gone abroad for work, 34% went to Saudi Arabia, which has been the top destination since overseas employment began.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report (BMET data implied)

facts.statement: In the five months to May 2025, 73% of workers who left Bangladesh for work went to Saudi Arabia: about 300,000 (3 lakh) of 420,000 (4 lakh 20 thousand) total departures.
facts.source_in_article: BMET

facts.statement: As of June 2025 the United Arab Emirates, Bangladesh's second largest labour market, was closed to Bangladeshi workers.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: Oman, Bangladesh's third largest labour market, had been closed to Bangladeshi workers since 2024 and was still closed in June 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: Malaysia's labour market has been closed to Bangladeshi workers since June 2024; as of June 2025 the two countries were in talks to reopen it quickly.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: As of June 2025 Bangladesh was unable to send workers to Japan and South Korea in the numbers demanded, and the potential to send workers to Europe was also not being used well.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: Saudi Arabia kept visas (for Bangladeshi workers) closed during June 2025; the country was expected to make a new announcement in July 2025. BAIRA's former secretary general Ali Haider Chowdhury said Saudi visas were closed for one month, new demand had also fallen, and Saudi Arabia might introduce more screening in worker recruitment.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Haider Chowdhury, former BAIRA secretary general; sector sources

facts.statement: Sector people said Saudi demand rose because of large infrastructure construction for the 2034 football World Cup, which Saudi Arabia will host, but demand had already begun to fall by mid-2025.
facts.source_in_article: migration sector people

facts.statement: BMET data: over 1.1 million (11 lakh) workers went abroad from Bangladesh in 2022, 1.3 million (13 lakh) in 2023, and 1.0 million (10 lakh) in 2024, a fall of 300,000.
facts.source_in_article: BMET

facts.statement: BMET data: in the first five months of 2025, 420,000 workers left Bangladesh; 300,000 went to Saudi Arabia, 40,000 to Qatar (second) and more than 26,000 to Singapore.
facts.source_in_article: BMET

facts.statement: Sector people said most workers going to Saudi Arabia obtain the recruitment demand letter through acquaintances or relatives; a class of brokers has grown up around this who pass off fake appointment letters, so some people reach Saudi Arabia and find no work and are cheated.
facts.source_in_article: migration sector people

facts.statement: BMET data on Bangladeshi women going abroad for work: 105,466 in 2022; 76,108 in 2023 (down 28%); 61,158 in 2024 (down 20%); 24,617 in the first five months of 2025, of whom 17,786 went to Saudi Arabia and about 4,500 to Jordan.
facts.source_in_article: BMET

facts.statement: In 2022-2024 more than 3.4 million (34 lakh) Bangladeshi workers went abroad, of whom fewer than 250,000 were women. From 2015 to 2019 more than 100,000 women went abroad every year; the number fell in 2020 because of the pandemic, rose in the next two years, and has fallen for two years.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report (BMET data)

facts.statement: Most Bangladeshi women migrants go to Middle Eastern countries as domestic workers; some return after torture and abuse, and there are allegations of sexual abuse, which is reducing women's interest in going.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: Sumaiya Islam, executive director of Bangladesh Nari Sramik Kendra (BNSK), said necessary support for women workers in the Middle East has not been ensured, that the income from domestic work in Saudi Arabia is small compared with the labour required, that there are various complaints, so women's interest has fallen; and that Middle Eastern countries are taking workers from African countries as an alternative source.
facts.source_in_article: Sumaiya Islam, BNSK

facts.statement: Shakirul Islam, chairperson of Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program (OKUP), said the proposed (2025-26) budget cut the allocation for the migration sector below the previous level, that there is little prospect of overseas employment growing, and no progress in opening new labour markets.
facts.source_in_article: Shakirul Islam, OKUP

facts.statement: Sector people said the main reason the overseas labour market is shrinking is dependence on single countries: workers go in huge numbers to one country, problems arise, that market closes for several years, and sending shifts to another country.
facts.source_in_article: migration sector people

headline_en: Why the execution of two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia is a final warning bell
summary_en: A column by Helal Mohiuddin on the execution in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, of two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam Basir and Sweety (Siti) Akhtar, reported in mid-October 2026, which Dhaka says it did not know about in advance. It reviews how Bangladesh's missions handle prisoners and death-row cases, explains qisas, blood money, hadd and ta'zir in Saudi law, and contrasts Bangladesh's 2015 domestic-worker deal (800 riyal wage) with the protections Indonesia, the Philippines, India and Sri Lanka negotiated. It recommends death-penalty case monitoring cells in every mission, Wage Earners' Welfare Fund money for lawyers, interpreters and blood money, and a prisoner transfer treaty with Saudi Arabia.

facts.statement: Two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam Basir and Sweety (Siti) Akhtar, were executed in Makkah, Saudi Arabia; newspapers of 16 October 2026 reported that Dhaka had not known about the executions. The offence was described as an 'immoral relationship' (possibly zina/adultery) and the court sentenced them under ta'zir (the judge's discretionary punishment).
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin, citing newspapers

facts.statement: After the Saudi Press Agency reported the executions, the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah sent a letter to the Saudi foreign ministry on 15 October 2026. A Jeddah consulate official said they had received no notification or diplomatic note about the trial or the carrying out of the sentence; the Saudi statement gave only the two names, without iqama or passport details.
facts.source_in_article: newspapers quoted by the columnist; a Jeddah consulate official

facts.statement: According to the Daily Star of 19 October 2026, Saudi authorities gave (Bangladesh) a list of about 2,500 prisoners in September 2026 that included the names of Nazrul and Sweety; the list did not mention a death sentence, and the offence of one was written as 'adultery'. The columnist says Saudi Arabia had asked for information on the prisoners in September.
facts.source_in_article: Daily Star, 19 October 2026, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: One or two newspapers reported that the case against the two executed Bangladeshis ran for several months in a Jeddah court and that two Bangladeshis worked as interpreters in it, yet the mission did not learn of it.
facts.source_in_article: newspapers cited by the columnist

facts.statement: Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia are both parties to the 1963 Vienna Convention on Consular Relations; Article 36 obliges prompt notification of the consulate, though in some cases the prisoner has to request it.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: Through the efforts of Bangladesh's embassies, 49,503 Bangladeshis were released from (prisons in) 20 countries between 2012 and 2016, including 17,335 from Saudi Arabia and about 5,000 from the UAE. The columnist says most of the Saudi returnees were workers whose iqama or visa had expired, and their 'release' amounted to arranging an air ticket and an out-pass.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: The Bangladesh consulate in Saudi Arabia regularly applies for royal pardon for Bangladeshi prisoners who are not held for serious crimes.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: Every year during Ramadan, the two Eids and the anniversary of the Prophet's death, Middle Eastern countries give prisoners and minor offenders the chance to return home under general amnesties. In 2012 King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia freed large numbers of prisoners through a general amnesty and by paying compensation and blood money, one reason many convicted Bangladeshis were returned that year.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: In 2021 the governor of Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province spared a Bangladeshi from a death sentence and arranged for him to be sent home.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: On 7 October 2011 eight Bangladeshi workers were beheaded in Saudi Arabia for the murder of an Egyptian guard. Bangladesh repeatedly appealed for pardon and offered blood money, but the guard's family refused to accept it.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: In Saudi 'qisas' (murder) cases the power to pardon lies only with the victim's family; the Sharia court has no power over it. Blood money is the last resort: if the victim's family demands money as compensation, it is paid, and the family agrees to forgive, even a person sentenced to death is released.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: In October 2011 the Dammam high court asked what steps the Bangladesh government was taking to bring back about 500 Bangladeshis held in Dammam prison; Saudi Arabia was willing to return minor offenders under a general amnesty, but because of the embassy's indifference tickets and out-passes were not arranged, and the administrative documents it prepared had many errors and inconsistencies.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: In July 2024, 57 Bangladeshis were convicted in a speedy trial in the UAE for anti-Hasina protests; 3 got life and 53 got 10 years' imprisonment (figures as printed). After the Hasina government fell, the UAE president pardoned them within a week of a phone call with interim government head Dr Yunus.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: Bangladesh has signed sentenced-prisoner transfer agreements with only two countries: India (2010) and the UAE (2014). It has none with Saudi Arabia; India signed such an agreement with Saudi Arabia in 2010.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: According to a report by Lutful Haque in the English edition of BD Pratidin on 22 February 2024, Saudi ambassador Essa bin Yousef Al-Duhailan called on the home ministry and then home minister Asaduzzaman Khan Kamal said the Saudi government was interested in a prisoner repatriation agreement with Bangladesh, that Bangladesh had no objection and would consider a proposal if received. As of the column (October 2026) no such agreement is reported.
facts.source_in_article: BD Pratidin 22 February 2024, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: The columnist says that in a death-penalty case an embassy must know from the day of arrest: what the charge sheet says, whether there is a lawyer, whether the interpreter is neutral, when the appeal is, what the verdict is, and whether the family knows.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: Indonesia: after domestic worker Ruyati was beheaded in Saudi Arabia in 2011 without notice, Jakarta suspended sending domestic workers to Saudi Arabia. In 2014 the Indonesian government itself paid about USD 1.8-1.9 million in blood money to save another worker, Satinah, whose execution was postponed five times; President Yudhoyono wrote three letters to the Saudi authorities.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: The Philippines demanded a minimum wage for domestic workers in 2011 and Saudi Arabia stopped hiring; Riyadh finally agreed to USD 400 a month. Under the agreement signed in May 2013, a minimum salary of 1,500 riyals, a weekly day off, paid leave, no withholding of passports, free communication and a 24-hour assistance system are mandatory for Filipino domestic workers.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: After the body of Filipino domestic worker Joanna Demafelis was found in a freezer in Kuwait in 2018, the Philippines completely stopped sending workers to Kuwait; the agreement signed on 11 May 2018 secured workers' right to keep their own phone, a 24-hour hotline and a special police unit to help the embassy with rescues.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: India's domestic worker recruitment agreement with Saudi Arabia of 2 January 2014 banned deducting recruitment cost from wages and provided a bank account in the worker's name, 24-hour assistance and an exit visa in emergencies; Sri Lanka signed a similar agreement the same month.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: Under the domestic worker agreement Bangladesh signed with Saudi Arabia on 10 February 2015, the wage was set at only 800 riyals, about half the Philippine rate (1,500 riyals).
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: Tasneem Siddiqui of RMMRU said at the time (2015) that Bangladesh had bargaining power because India, Sri Lanka and Indonesia had stopped sending workers to Saudi Arabia, and demanded that the embassy phone each woman worker at least once a month; the BAIRA president admitted they had prioritised opening the market.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin, citing Tasneem Siddiqui (RMMRU) and the BAIRA president

facts.statement: The columnist explains that Islamic criminal law has three tracks: hadd, qisas and ta'zir. Zina (adultery) falls under hadd, which requires four reliable adult witnesses with no criminal record and is waived if there is any doubt; the accused may retract a confession. Ta'zir (discretionary punishment) is normally for minor offences and many scholars limit it to ten lashes, but Saudi Arabia has previously given the death penalty under ta'zir in a few drug cases, which drew international criticism.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

facts.statement: The columnist recommends four steps to the foreign ministry: (1) a list and monitoring cell for death-penalty cases in every mission, with monthly updates from prisons and courts; (2) a set allocation from the Wage Earners' Welfare Fund for lawyers, independent interpreters and, if needed, blood money, as Indonesia has done; (3) revive and quickly conclude the prisoner transfer agreement Saudi Arabia itself proposed; (4) write separate consular notification and legal aid clauses into every future labour agreement.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Helal Mohiuddin

headline_en: Government working to reopen the closed Malaysian labour market: expatriates' welfare secretary
summary_en: On Wednesday 16 September 2026 expatriates' welfare secretary Md. Mokhtar Ahmed said the process to reopen Malaysia's closed labour market in a transparent way is ongoing and the method of sending workers will be announced formally once settled. BAIRA members handed him a memorandum demanding equal opportunity for all valid agencies including the 312 listed ones, an end to the syndicate, lower costs and a BOESL one-stop service. He said a mobile court had sealed the office of 'Triple A Overseas', fined it and seized three boxes of passports.

facts.statement: As of 16 September 2026 Malaysia's labour market was still closed to Bangladeshi workers; expatriates' welfare secretary Md. Mokhtar Ahmed said the process of reopening it is ongoing, the administrative work on which process will be used to send workers is under way, and it will be announced formally once confirmed.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Mokhtar Ahmed, Secretary, Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment

facts.statement: BAIRA members submitted a memorandum to the expatriates' welfare secretary on 16 September 2026 demanding, for Malaysia: equal opportunity for all valid and eligible recruiting agencies including the 312 listed agencies, an end to syndicate and monopoly, a significant cut in migration cost, full transparency in recruitment, opening to all eligible medical centres, and a one-stop service through BOESL.
facts.source_in_article: BAIRA memorandum

facts.statement: The expatriates' welfare ministry ran a mobile court against illegal and fraudulent activity, sealed the office of 'Triple A Overseas' (ত্রিপল আ ওভারসিজ), imposed a fine and seized three boxes of passports.
facts.source_in_article: Secretary Md. Mokhtar Ahmed

facts.statement: The secretary said care is needed that no middlemen profit from the Malaysia reopening and that the ministry is taking a hard line to protect ordinary workers from brokers and fraud rings.
facts.source_in_article: Secretary Md. Mokhtar Ahmed

facts.statement: The secretary said several minister-level meetings between Bangladesh and Malaysia had already been held on reopening the labour market, and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman raised it in bilateral talks with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar during his first foreign trip.
facts.source_in_article: Secretary Md. Mokhtar Ahmed

headline_en: Why are fewer women workers going abroad
summary_en: An opinion column by Dr Selim Reza of North South University on the steady fall in Bangladeshi women going abroad for work, from 105,466 in 2022 to 61,977 in 2025. He argues policy has focused on restricting women rather than protecting them, that women's migration is confined to domestic work in a few Middle Eastern countries, and that skills and reintegration are neglected. He proposes six policy changes.

facts.statement: Government figures on Bangladeshi women going abroad for work: 105,466 in 2022; 76,108 in 2023; 61,158 in 2024; 61,977 in 2025, which is still about 41% lower than 2022.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University, citing government statistics

facts.statement: In 2025 more than 1.1 million (11 lakh) Bangladeshi workers went abroad, of whom women were only about 5.5%.
facts.source_in_article: BMET, 2026, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: Over the past decade there have been many incidents in Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Oman and other countries of Bangladeshi women workers facing torture, sexual violence, non-payment of wages, passport confiscation, forced labour or unnatural death; many returned cheated and abused, with debt, physical illness or mental trauma.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: The columnist says Bangladesh's policy response to women's insecurity abroad has at various times been extra administrative control and restrictions on women's migration (age-limit conditions, administrative approvals, restrictive rules) rather than strengthening protection.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: Most Bangladeshi women going abroad still go as domestic workers to a few Middle Eastern countries: Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Oman, the United Arab Emirates and Lebanon; no effective new destinations have been found outside this limited market.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: There is still no integrated, open database on what Bangladeshi women workers do abroad, how much they earn, how many are abused, how many upskill and move sectors, or what they do after return.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: The columnist says demand for skilled women is growing in Europe, Japan, South Korea, Canada and Australia, where the elderly population is rising, in health care, the care economy, elderly care, hospitality, agriculture, food processing and tech-based services (trained caregivers, nursing assistants, hotel workers, technical workers), but Bangladesh has not produced skilled women workers to match; most departing women have limited formal skills, weak language ability and no skills recognition.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: Thousands of women who return from abroad cannot restart their lives because of social stigma, trauma, financial instability and lack of skills recognition; reintegration is weak, entrepreneurship opportunities limited and mental health services almost absent.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: Bangladesh now earns more than USD 35 billion a year in remittances.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: The columnist proposes six policy changes for women migrants: (1) move beyond the Middle East domestic-worker market to new destinations, skills and occupations, with a special strategy for Europe, East Asia and other high-income countries; (2) large public investment in international-standard language, caregiving, health care, digital and technical training before departure; (3) reduce dependence on brokers through a transparent, digital recruitment system to cut cost and fraud; (4) rebuild bilateral labour agreements to cover labour rights, social protection, complaint resolution, insurance, legal aid and safe workplaces; (5) treat returnee women's reintegration as economic reinvestment with skills recognition, easy loans, entrepreneurship support and mental health care, as part of national migration policy; (6) treat women's migration as part of national economic strategy.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

key_quote_bn: ২০২৫ সালে সামান্য বেড়ে ৬১ হাজার ৯৭৭ হলেও তা এখনো ২০২২ সালের তুলনায় প্রায় ৪১ শতাংশ কম।

headline_en: Rights of women migrant workers and safe migration
summary_en: Proceedings of a roundtable on women migrant workers' rights and safe migration held on 5 May 2026 at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka, organised by Badabon Sangho and Prothom Alo. The Wage Earners' Welfare Board official set out membership fees and the amounts of its sickness, disability, injury, death and insurance benefits and its legal aid through 22 law firms in 12 countries; BOESL described its recruitment process and zero-cost sending of women garment workers to Jordan since 2010. The state minister listed planned measures (district one-stop service, Probashi Card, standard migration cost, agency grading), and NGOs, ILO, IOM, UNDP and returnee women's leaders gave data and criticism on training, sub-agents, deaths of women abroad and reintegration.

facts.statement: A roundtable titled 'Rights of women migrant workers and safe migration' was held on 5 May 2026 at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka, organised by Badabon Sangho and Prothom Alo; participants included State Minister Md. Nurul Haque MP and officials of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board, BOESL, ILO, IOM, UNDP, BILS, RMMRU, BRAC, BNSK, WARBE and returnee women's organisations.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo

facts.statement: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Md. Nurul Haque said legal remedies for women migrants used to be limited but agreements with some countries have now created scope to file cases and recover compensation; incidents of insecurity are more common in some Middle Eastern countries.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister Md. Nurul Haque

facts.statement: The state minister said there are various problems with the labour market, syndicates, tests and recruitment systems in Malaysia, Korea, Saudi Arabia and other countries, and that complaints of irregularities and extra costs arise in places; the government wants to reduce these and ensure transparency.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister Md. Nurul Haque

facts.statement: The state minister said online services for expatriates' welfare have been launched so that dependence on brokers falls gradually, that attention will be given to modernising the Technical Training Centres (TTCs), and that similar training given by different ministries needs to be coordinated.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister Md. Nurul Haque

facts.statement: The state minister said the government will send women workers abroad after skilling them, appoint legal firms abroad for their protection, ensure digital banking facilities, and form a special fund for rehabilitating returnees (stated as plans).
facts.source_in_article: State Minister Md. Nurul Haque

facts.statement: The state minister said planned measures include: a one-stop service at district level by bringing the manpower office, Probashi Kallyan Bank and welfare centres into the same building, to ease services for women wanting to go abroad; a 'Probashi Card' for expatriates; fixing a standard migration cost; and a grading system to identify good recruiting agencies.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister Md. Nurul Haque

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board says it takes responsibility for the full welfare of a woman or man worker from the moment they pass immigration, and their family members at home also come under its support. If a worker abroad falls ill, goes to jail or is in danger, legal assistance is given through the labour wing (of the Bangladesh mission).
facts.source_in_article: Dr A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, joint secretary and Director (Finance and Budget), Wage Earners' Welfare Board

facts.statement: Anyone, documented or undocumented, can become a member of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board by paying BDT 400. (The same official later refers to membership 'with BDT 300' in the context of death benefits; the article prints both figures.)
facts.source_in_article: Dr A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, joint secretary and Director (Finance and Budget), Wage Earners' Welfare Board

facts.statement: A Wage Earners' Welfare Board member who applies because of illness within one year of returning home is given one-off assistance of up to BDT 200,000 (2 lakh).
facts.source_in_article: Dr A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, joint secretary and Director (Finance and Budget), Wage Earners' Welfare Board

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board pays an allowance of BDT 2,000 per month for up to seven years for a disabled child of a migrant, for up to two disabled children per family.
facts.source_in_article: Dr A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, joint secretary and Director (Finance and Budget), Wage Earners' Welfare Board

facts.statement: For injury or loss of a limb abroad, assistance of up to BDT 400,000 (4 lakh) is given against a premium of BDT 500. Under life insurance there is also a five-year policy for BDT 1,000.
facts.source_in_article: Dr A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, joint secretary and Director (Finance and Budget), Wage Earners' Welfare Board

facts.statement: In case of death abroad, if the worker had membership (stated as BDT 300), the body is brought home from any country in the world and BDT 35,000 is given for burial and transport costs; an additional BDT 300,000 (3 lakh) is given to the heirs, and if there is insurance up to a further BDT 1,000,000 (10 lakh) can be received.
facts.source_in_article: Dr A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, joint secretary and Director (Finance and Budget), Wage Earners' Welfare Board

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board helps recover dues owed abroad through 22 law firms in 12 countries.
facts.source_in_article: Dr A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, joint secretary and Director (Finance and Budget), Wage Earners' Welfare Board

facts.statement: Under the reintegration policy, more than 239,000 (2 lakh 39 thousand) people have so far been given training, counselling and financial assistance; among women, 33 have completed RPL (recognition of prior learning) in driving.
facts.source_in_article: Dr A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, joint secretary and Director (Finance and Budget), Wage Earners' Welfare Board

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board official said that with three to six months of training a person can go abroad as a skilled worker, and that big opportunities are opening for women not only in garments or caregiving but also in construction, electrical work and welding.
facts.source_in_article: Dr A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, joint secretary and Director (Finance and Budget), Wage Earners' Welfare Board

facts.statement: Syed Sultan Uddin Ahmed, executive director of BILS, said the recommendations of the Labour Reform Commission's expert team on migrant workers should be the basis for fundamental reform, that a five-year plan with a roadmap is needed, that the state must set minimum standards instead of bargaining prices down before entering a market, and that the law should give migrant workers the right to organise, be represented and sit on committees. He said Nepal's government has arranged housing, transport and security for domestic workers, which reduced abuse.
facts.source_in_article: Syed Sultan Uddin Ahmed, BILS

facts.statement: Razekuzzaman Ratan, president of Samajtantrik Sramik Front, said the war situation in the Middle East could have a big impact on the labour market and may increase security risks and abuse, so advance analysis of which kinds of women workers will be in demand over the next year, and special attention to protection, are needed.
facts.source_in_article: Razekuzzaman Ratan

facts.statement: Razekuzzaman Ratan said women's hard-earned money often does not stay under their own control, leaving them in financial uncertainty on return; women's full right over their earnings must be ensured and they should be trained in remittance management. He also called for investment protection, small business support, an effective database, police-station-based help desks and protection from harassment for returnee women, and accountability of recruiting agencies and sub-agents.
facts.source_in_article: Razekuzzaman Ratan

facts.statement: IOM's Farzana Shahnaz said that with funding from the Government of Italy a pilot initiative has been taken to deliver migration information through Union Digital Centres (UDCs), the government's grassroots service centres, through which pre-migration preparation training can be given; for lack of reliable information, village people depend on brokers.
facts.source_in_article: Farzana Shahnaz, National Programme Officer, IOM

facts.statement: IOM's Farzana Shahnaz said people must understand before going how much it will cost, how much they will earn, how long they will stay and what the final gain is, because people often go on high-cost loans and the income is nearly used up repaying the debt; the government's pre-departure module should be implemented more effectively.
facts.source_in_article: Farzana Shahnaz, IOM

facts.statement: Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) has worked since 1984 as a government manpower exporting company under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment.
facts.source_in_article: Nu-Emong Marma Mong, Deputy Manager (Overseas Recruitment), BOESL

facts.statement: BOESL's process: it starts when a government-to-government agreement is made or an employer assigns BOESL to recruit. After demand is received from the employer, labour wing officials at the Bangladesh embassy verify it; if satisfactory, the information is published as a notice and a test is held with the employer or their local representative present; after the test BOESL assists with all legal procedures for going abroad.
facts.source_in_article: Nu-Emong Marma Mong, Deputy Manager (Overseas Recruitment), BOESL

facts.statement: Since 2010 BOESL has been sending women workers to Jordan's garment sector completely free of cost; BOESL officials handle everything from the medical and pre-departure training to getting to the airport.
facts.source_in_article: Nu-Emong Marma Mong, Deputy Manager (Overseas Recruitment), BOESL

facts.statement: BOESL says it announces the fixed migration cost for each country in advance, so those who go through BOESL cannot be cheated. Its pre-departure training teaches behaviour with the employer, emergency contacts and even the rules of air travel.
facts.source_in_article: Nu-Emong Marma Mong, Deputy Manager (Overseas Recruitment), BOESL

facts.statement: ILO's Rahnuma Salam Khan said a 2025 government rule (the article uses both 'policy' and 'rules') clearly set out the responsibilities and accountability of recruiting agencies and sub-agents in order to reduce migration cost, but its effective implementation or enforcement had not yet begun as of May 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Rahnuma Salam Khan, Senior National Programme Manager, ILO

facts.statement: An assessment of 40 Technical Training Centres (TTCs) found that training at TTCs under BMET is in many cases not fully consistent with the demand of overseas labour markets. There are separate TTCs for women. A 2016 policy said new labour markets where labour rights are protected should be sought, but there is no clear roadmap to implement it.
facts.source_in_article: Rahnuma Salam Khan, ILO

facts.statement: UNDP gender expert Sharmin Islam said people are sent abroad after three days of training, in which it is not possible to learn the language, understand the culture or gain practical job skills; women workers are often seen standing confused at the airport with no idea what to do, and the same happens to men.
facts.source_in_article: Sharmin Islam, UNDP Bangladesh

facts.statement: BNSK director S K Mojibul Haque said most (Bangladeshi) women workers abroad have to work 12 to 14 hours instead of 8 hours.
facts.source_in_article: S K Mojibul Haque, Director, BNSK

facts.statement: BNSK's director said women often do not get the service they want when they come to the DEMO office (district employment and manpower office), TTCs and Probashi Kallyan Kendra (welfare centres), and these must be made women-friendly; he also proposed involving expatriate communities in destination countries to monitor women working inside homes, and state monitoring of brokers' and recruiting agents' false publicity on digital media (the printed sentence on this is garbled).
facts.source_in_article: S K Mojibul Haque, BNSK

facts.statement: According to Wage Earners' Welfare Board data, about 799 to 800 women migrants came home dead in the past 8 years; in most cases the cause is given as heart attack or physical illness, sometimes suicide, but the true cause is not known.
facts.source_in_article: Jasiya Khatun, Director, WARBE Development Foundation, citing Wage Earners' Welfare Board data

facts.statement: According to BMET data, more than 1 million (10 lakh) Bangladeshi women are currently working abroad, though the number of women migrating has fallen in the past few years; the main reasons given are the lack of new labour markets, too few women-friendly workplaces, and physical, mental and sexual abuse.
facts.source_in_article: Jasiya Khatun, WARBE Development Foundation, citing BMET

facts.statement: WARBE's Jasiya Khatun said that at present there is compensation for death or permanent injury but insurance should also be arranged for complicated and long-term illness; she called for the list of employers in the Middle East to be strictly monitored by the ministry and embassies and risky employers to be blacklisted.
facts.source_in_article: Jasiya Khatun, WARBE Development Foundation

facts.statement: RMMRU programme director Marina Sultana said women currently make up about 13.5% of total migration (figure as stated by her), and that Bangladesh is failing to hold markets such as Hong Kong and Singapore and to create new markets such as caregiving.
facts.source_in_article: Marina Sultana, RMMRU

facts.statement: RMMRU said it helped the government frame rules that legally provide for the registration of sub-agents, but this has not yet been fully implemented; RMMRU also worked on alternative dispute resolution to make BMET's arbitration process more transparent.
facts.source_in_article: Marina Sultana, RMMRU

facts.statement: Badabon Sangho, which began in 2016 and was formally registered around 2018-19, works on women migrant workers' rights; in 2020 it worked with UN Women support on women workers who returned during Covid in Keraniganj, and in 2024-25 it formed women-led forums in six districts: Cumilla, Sunamganj, Gopalganj, Manikganj, Narsingdi and Pabna, with a larger forum formed in December 2025 that regularly hears migration problems.
facts.source_in_article: Lipi Rahman, Executive Director, Badabon Sangho

facts.statement: BRAC Migration Programme coordinator Md. Harun-Or-Rashid said that from BRAC's work experience in 42 countries, Nepal, Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam are far ahead in protecting their citizens and have stopped sending workers when necessary, while Bangladesh still sends workers with a weak database, little training and an irregular process.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Harun-Or-Rashid, BRAC Migration Programme

facts.statement: According to BMET data, more than 1,095,000 (10 lakh 95 thousand) Bangladeshi women went abroad between 2001 and 2022.
facts.source_in_article: Fariha Jesmin, Programme Manager, Badabon Sangho, citing BMET

facts.statement: A 2025 study by Badabon Sangho in Dhaka, Manikganj, Gopalganj, Sunamganj, Narsingdi, Cumilla and Pabna found 27.6% of women migrated without having any source of income, indicating forced migration; many took high-interest loans or sold assets, and abroad they faced low pay, loss of control of their passport, long working hours and abuse.
facts.source_in_article: Badabon Sangho 2025 study, presented by Fariha Jesmin

facts.statement: Badabon Sangho's Fariha Jesmin said risks remain because of the kafala system, broker syndicates and lack of control, and called for kafala reform, digital wage protection, fast labour courts, safe housing and a reintegration policy.
facts.source_in_article: Fariha Jesmin, Badabon Sangho

facts.statement: Sheikh Romana, general secretary of Bangladesh Ovibashi Mohila Sramik Association (BOMSA), said that of about 2,200 (recruiting) agencies, 1,100 are legal, yet ethical recruitment has not become real.
facts.source_in_article: Sheikh Romana, BOMSA

facts.statement: Bangladesh Ovibashi Mohila Sramik Association holds courtyard meetings at grassroots level and gives pre-departure training that teaches keeping money and opening two (bank) accounts. Its general secretary said many women return abused with children, for whom the state must take responsibility, and that embassies have too few staff.
facts.source_in_article: Sheikh Romana, BOMSA

facts.statement: Before going abroad, a three-day basic training is given at the district employment office, teaching mainly some elementary language, culture and rules, but not in-depth training on the reality of the work, risks and long-term situation.
facts.source_in_article: Mahmuda Sultana, general secretary, Ovibashi Nari Sramik Federation (returnee)

facts.statement: Mahmuda Sultana of the Ovibashi Nari Sramik Federation said many women do not go abroad by choice but under family pressure, get hardly any reintegration support after returning from harassment and abuse, and that those who return aged 45-50 are in a pitiful state; she asked for a government card or allowance structure for returnee women workers.
facts.source_in_article: Mahmuda Sultana, Ovibashi Nari Sramik Federation

facts.statement: The roundtable's recommendations: frame and implement a dignified, safe migration policy for the whole migration cycle; make modern, market-based skills training compulsory; increase women's participation in new sectors beyond caregiving including health care, construction, electrical and welding; introduce strict licensing, grading and accountability for recruiting agencies and sub-agents; ensure women's full financial right and control over their earnings and train them in remittance management; ensure gender sensitivity in the migration process.
facts.source_in_article: roundtable recommendations

headline_en: Oman's labour market to open soon for Bangladeshi workers
summary_en: Oman's labour minister assured Bangladesh's expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul, at a meeting on the sidelines of the Global Labour Market Conference in Saudi Arabia, that work visas for Bangladeshi workers, suspended since 2023 for unskilled and semi-skilled workers, would be reopened within the next two months. The Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh reported this on Tuesday 27 January 2026. Asif Nazrul also asked for more hiring of professionals, a joint technical committee meeting in Muscat and signing of a finalised MoU, and thanked Oman for letting irregular Bangladeshi workers regularise without fines.

facts.statement: The Oman government assured Bangladesh that work visas for Bangladeshi workers, which have been closed, will be reopened within the next two months; Oman's labour minister Mahad bin Said bin Ali Baowain (printed in full as মাহাদ বিন সাঈদ বিন আলী বাওয়াইন সালিম আল-বুসাইদি) gave this assurance to adviser Asif Nazrul at a meeting on the sidelines of the Global Labour Market Conference in Saudi Arabia. The minister expressed it as a hope after reviewing the situation.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh notice / Second Secretary (Press) Asaduzzaman Khan

facts.statement: Oman's labour minister said new visas for unskilled and semi-skilled workers had been temporarily stopped since 2023 in order to prioritise the regularisation of irregular and undocumented migrant workers.
facts.source_in_article: Oman's labour minister, via Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh notice

facts.statement: The Oman government has given irregular Bangladeshi workers the opportunity to regularise their status without paying fines; adviser Asif Nazrul thanked the Omani minister for this.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh notice / Second Secretary (Press) Asaduzzaman Khan

facts.statement: Adviser Asif Nazrul asked Oman's labour minister for special cooperation to increase recruitment of Bangladeshi engineers, doctors, nurses and other highly skilled professionals, and requested quick withdrawal of the suspension on general workers.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh notice / Second Secretary (Press) Asaduzzaman Khan

facts.statement: Bangladesh proposed convening a Joint Technical Committee (JTC) meeting in Muscat in the first half of 2026 and urged Oman to quickly sign the already finalised memorandum of understanding (MoU) on labour cooperation.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh notice / Second Secretary (Press) Asaduzzaman Khan

facts.statement: Asif Nazrul told the Omani minister the Bangladesh government's steps include more use of technology in the migration process, proper skills verification before sending workers, pre-departure training on the destination country's language, culture and law, and controlling migration cost through legal reform.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh notice / Second Secretary (Press) Asaduzzaman Khan

headline_en: Few workers are going to Italy, a promising labour market: why
summary_en: A May 2025 report on why legal labour migration from Bangladesh to Italy collapsed from 16,879 in 2023 to 1,164 in 2024. Italy tightened visas after fake job offers and workers arriving without language or skills; the Italian embassy in Dhaka takes over a year to verify some applications and has returned passports without visas. The article gives the history of the Italy corridor, the 6 May 2025 Bangladesh-Italy migration and mobility MoU, and the EU-funded Talent Partnership project.

facts.statement: BMET data on Bangladeshi workers going to Italy legally: 653 in 2021; 7,594 in 2022; 16,879 in 2023; only 1,164 in 2024; and 1,246 in the first four months of 2025.
facts.source_in_article: BMET

facts.statement: After being closed for seven straight years, a bilateral agreement on worker recruitment was signed between Bangladesh and Italy in 2020 and sending workers resumed from 2021.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: The Italian government tightened visa issuance (from 2024) because many Bangladeshis could not secure employment in Italy without language and technical knowledge and because of allegations of fake appointment letters (job offers).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: Even when a work appointment letter has arrived, the Italian embassy in Dhaka is taking a long time on verification before giving a visa; some workers have waited more than a year. After workers protested in 2024 about passports being held for a long time, many passports were returned; passports will be taken in again once verification of the appointment letter is finished.
facts.source_in_article: people concerned (sector sources)

facts.statement: According to Italbangla association sources, about 100,000 (1 lakh) workers trying to go to Italy got caught in visa complications in 2024 after the tightening; some got passports back without a visa, and they recently gathered and protested in the Kakrail area (Dhaka).
facts.source_in_article: Italbangla Samannay O Unnayan Samity sources

facts.statement: Italbangla association sources say 80% of workers who went to Italy on legal work visas between 2020 and 2023 later became irregular. Shah Md. Taifur Rahman of Probashi Unnayan Samity likewise said 80% of workers coming to Italy do not become legal because they do not know the language or the work.
facts.source_in_article: Italbangla Samannay O Unnayan Samity; Shah Md. Taifur Rahman

facts.statement: Shah Md. Taifur Rahman, executive director of Probashi Unnayan Samity, said those who learn Italian are still getting visas easily, so workers should be sent with skills and language training.
facts.source_in_article: Shah Md. Taifur Rahman, Probashi Unnayan Samity

facts.statement: People concerned say no language other than Italian is used in Italy, so working there without learning Italian is hard; and that a foreign worker must work for at least 5 years in the (European) country that gave the work permit, after which, on getting a residence permit, they can work in another country; going to another country before that makes the worker illegal.
facts.source_in_article: people concerned (sector sources)

facts.statement: Workers without even minimum technical skills sign up to go to Italy in exchange for money; there are also allegations of fake appointment letters.
facts.source_in_article: people concerned (sector sources)

facts.statement: People concerned warn that if the legal route to Italy is disrupted, the tendency to enter Italy illegally by crossing the Mediterranean may rise.
facts.source_in_article: people concerned

facts.statement: History per Italbangla Samannay O Unnayan Samity (formed 1992 to serve Bangladeshis in Italy): Bangladeshis began going to Italy in the 1980s; irregular workers first got legal status in 1987, and later in several rounds; Italy first included Bangladesh in its foreign worker quota in 2003; in 2011 Italy wanted to send back some irregular workers but could not for lack of an agreement; Italy cancelled Bangladesh's quota in 2012 and sending stopped from the next year, which increased irregular travel; total Bangladeshi migrants in Italy passed 200,000 in 2015.
facts.source_in_article: Italbangla Samannay O Unnayan Samity

facts.statement: A memorandum of understanding on migration and mobility between Bangladesh and Italy was signed in Dhaka on 6 May 2025. Adviser Asif Nazrul said Italy will take workers in two ways, seasonal and non-seasonal; a joint technical committee meeting once a year is planned; work is under way on Italian language training at Technical Training Centres; and quick processing of visa applications pending at the Italian embassy was discussed with Italy.
facts.source_in_article: Adviser Asif Nazrul

facts.statement: The EU-funded EUR 3 million (30 lakh euro) Talent Partnership project formally started in December 2024 to supply skilled workers to the European labour market by legal routes; the ILO, the expatriates' welfare ministry and BMET are to implement it over three years (2024-27).
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo report

headline_en: What remittance fighters want to see from the BNP government
summary_en: An opinion column by Dr Selim Reza marking the BNP government's 100th day, reviewing its election pledges on migration (new labour markets, skills, digital registration, a target of sending 10 million skilled workers abroad) against what migrants expected. He says a worker often spends BDT 3-8 lakh to go abroad, mostly to brokers, and that so far broker influence, costs, new markets and welfare services show little visible change.

facts.statement: A worker going abroad from Bangladesh often has to spend up to about BDT 3-8 lakh (300,000 to 800,000 taka); a large part goes to brokers, middlemen or unregulated agents who are not accountable, so workers spend the first few months, even a whole year, abroad just repaying debt.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: The columnist says migrant workers, working extra without breaks day after day to repay migration debt, fall physically ill and many die.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: In its 2026 election manifesto the BNP promised to find new labour markets to reduce dependence on the Middle East (Europe, East Asia and other regions), modern skills training, modernised remittance channels that are fast, safe and low-cost, strict control of middlemen and transparent recruitment, a digital registration system for the whole migration process, and set a target of sending one crore (10 million) skilled workers abroad.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University, describing the BNP manifesto

facts.statement: The columnist says many Middle Eastern countries have tightened their labour policies and are prioritising local employment, and that the ongoing US-Israel and Iran war has put the whole Middle East labour market at new risk, reducing opportunities for Bangladeshi workers.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: Many Bangladeshi workers abroad face unpaid wages, workplace abuse or legal trouble, and embassy services are often inadequate so they do not get quick help.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: Illegal channels such as hundi remain popular for sending money home because they seem faster and sometimes more profitable; the complexity and cost of legal channels add to this.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: Migrants' expectations of the government as listed by the columnist: a broker-free, transparent migration system with drives against unlicensed agents and strict monitoring of licensed recruiting agencies; low-cost migration through state channels with a fixed, enforced cost and a 'zero-cost migration' model; new markets in Europe, East Asia and Africa through labour agreements and skill-based visas; technical and language training from school and college level; 24-hour help desks, legal aid cells and emergency response at embassies, possibly under a 'Probashi Card'; and more incentives and easier legal remittance via digital platforms and mobile banking.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: The columnist says the government since taking office has announced plans to digitise registration, the visa process and information management, stressed skills development programmes, and taken an initiative to introduce an international payment system for remittances.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: The columnist's assessment at the government's 100th day: broker influence is still visible, especially in rural areas where workers are easily cheated for lack of information; the cost of going abroad has not fallen noticeably; diplomatic progress on new labour markets is slow; and there is no visible change in expatriate welfare services, so workers in trouble abroad get the same limited help as before.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

headline_en: Iraq wants to take workers from Bangladesh: expatriates' welfare ministry
summary_en: The expatriates' welfare ministry said on Thursday 16 October 2025 that Iraq's government expressed deep interest in recruiting workers from Bangladesh at a two-day joint committee meeting in Dhaka on 13-14 October 2025, where a memorandum/agreement and a 'record of discussion' were signed. Decisions include recruitment through demand letters attested by the Bangladesh embassy, employment contracts signed before departure, and a Bangladeshi request to regularise irregular workers in Iraq under a general amnesty.

facts.statement: A two-day joint committee meeting of Bangladeshi and Iraqi delegations was held at the expatriates' welfare ministry in Dhaka on 13 and 14 October 2025, where the Iraqi government expressed deep interest in recruiting workers from Bangladesh; a memorandum of understanding (the article calls it a 'samjhota chukti') on this was signed, and a 'record of discussion' was signed at the end.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release, 16 October 2025

facts.statement: It was decided that the Iraqi government will take a role in recruiting Bangladeshis in various sectors in Iraq by issuing worker visas; the meeting discussed the feasibility of sending skilled, low-skilled and unskilled workers to Iraq.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release, 16 October 2025

facts.statement: Under the decisions of the October 2025 Bangladesh-Iraq meeting, workers will be recruited through demand letters sent by the Iraqi employer and attested by the Bangladesh embassy, and Bangladeshi workers wishing to go to Iraq will sign an employment contract before leaving for that country.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release, 16 October 2025

facts.statement: The Bangladesh embassy (in Iraq) will collect information on which sectors in Iraq have demand for workers and take the necessary steps to send workers.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release, 16 October 2025

facts.statement: The Iraqi delegation showed a positive attitude toward regularising irregular Bangladeshi workers in Iraq; the Bangladesh government will send a request letter to the Iraqi government through the foreign ministry to regularise irregular workers under a general amnesty. (This is a request, not a granted amnesty.)
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release, 16 October 2025

facts.statement: The Bangladesh-Iraq joint committee will meet at least once a year to ease the sending of Bangladeshis to Iraq.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release, 16 October 2025

facts.statement: The agreement was signed by Ahmadul Haque, additional secretary of the expatriates' welfare ministry, and for Iraq by Kazim Abdur Reza Khaiyun At-Wani (কাজিম আবদুর রেজা খাইয়ুন আত-ওয়ানি), director general of the department of media, Arab and international relations; senior secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan was present, and the Iraqi delegation earlier called on adviser Asif Nazrul.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release, 16 October 2025

headline_en: Why Bangladesh is failing in the international labour market
summary_en: A June 2024 opinion column by three North South University researchers on why Bangladesh keeps losing overseas labour markets, written after Malaysia stopped taking new Bangladeshi workers (approved workers could not enter after 31 May 2024) and the Maldives suspended recruitment from Bangladesh over fake documents and recruitment irregularities. They list eight causes including poor image, neglect of technical and language education, focus on numbers over rights, politicisation, syndicates (Malaysia since 2007), unaccountable recruiting agencies and unregulated brokers, and suggest licensing and monitoring brokers.

facts.statement: According to an announcement in March 2024, Malaysia is no longer taking new workers from Bangladesh, and many workers who had approvals could not enter Malaysia after 31 May 2024.
facts.source_in_article: columnists Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat (North South University)

facts.statement: The Maldives home ministry suspended recruitment of workers from Bangladesh because of submission of fake documents by recruiting firms, irregularities in recruitment and other reasons; the step is part of the Maldives' effort to curb illegal migration and of its changed labour policy.
facts.source_in_article: columnists Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat (North South University), citing Prothom Alo and The Business Standard, 2024

facts.statement: The columnists say Malaysia's step is meant to curb recruitment irregularities and frame proper policy, and is mainly part of re-evaluating its labour policy and filling the quota reserved for foreign workers under the 12th Malaysia Plan.
facts.source_in_article: columnists Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat (North South University), citing Prothom Alo and The Business Standard, 2024

facts.statement: Some palm oil producers in Malaysia often refrain from recruiting Bangladeshi workers; Bangladeshi migrants in Malaysia face trouble because migration costs are far above the government-fixed cost and because they lack a clear understanding of the recruitment process.
facts.source_in_article: columnists Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat (North South University)

facts.statement: According to BMET data, Bangladeshi migrants have been working in various countries since 1976.
facts.source_in_article: BMET, cited by the columnists

facts.statement: The columnists say syndicates have been formed under various governments to control Bangladesh's labour market, with Malaysia since 2007 as an example; influential individuals want to control the market to profit from migrant workers.
facts.source_in_article: columnists Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat (North South University)

facts.statement: The columnists say recruiting agencies help expand markets but migrants also face unethical and inhumane treatment in destination countries because of them and they have not been made accountable; political influence has been observed in BAIRA elections.
facts.source_in_article: columnists Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat (North South University)

facts.statement: The columnists say many migrants are cheated by brokers (dalals) and lose all their money, and suggest keeping brokers under a monitoring system, taking legal steps to license them and letting them work under existing law; one group has repeatedly refused to bring brokers within a legal framework and recommends punishment instead.
facts.source_in_article: columnists Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat (North South University)

facts.statement: Bangladeshi, Pakistani and Indian students in Kyrgyzstan were recently attacked by local people; Pakistani and Indian embassy staff acted very quickly to rescue their students, while Bangladesh embassy staff's efforts to help Bangladeshi students did not succeed, according to the columnists.
facts.source_in_article: columnists Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat (North South University)

facts.statement: The columnists say Bangladesh has neglected technical education and language skills (European schools teach children at least two foreign languages), that families see technical institutes as not respectable, and that policy talks stress sending maximum numbers and remittances rather than migrants' rights; reports on overseas demand do not say in which sectors demand exists, why, or whether it will last.
facts.source_in_article: columnists Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder, Selim Reza and K M Noor-E-Jannat (North South University)
