headline_en: Will the Makkah pact be of any use to Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia?
summary_en: An opinion column by Dr Selim Reza asking what the recently signed Makkah mutual defence pact (Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, with Turkey close to it) means for Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia. He says the pact is not a labour agreement and will not by itself improve wages, recruitment or conditions, but Bangladesh could use any decision to join as leverage to obtain a worker protection protocol, lower recruitment costs, contract verification, stronger consular capacity and published protection indicators. He notes long-standing complaints of high recruitment cost, contract substitution, unpaid wages, passport confiscation and abuse, and that Saudi domestic workers remain largely outside full labour law protection.

facts.statement: A mutual defence pact was recently signed in Makkah between Saudi Arabia and Pakistan (with Turkey's closeness noted); the columnist stresses it is a defence agreement, not a labour rights charter, and that even if Bangladesh joined there is no basis to expect Bangladeshi workers' pay to rise, employers to return passports, unpaid wages to be paid faster or abused women domestic workers to get legal protection overnight.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: Saudi Arabia has in recent years made some labour market reforms for foreign workers: certain categories of workers have more freedom to change jobs and to leave the country, but domestic workers are in many respects still outside full labour law protection; the ILO and rights activists are concerned about enforcement and accountability, not only changes in law.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: Long-standing complaints about Bangladeshi labour migration to Saudi Arabia listed by the columnist: excessive recruitment cost, dependence on brokers, mismatch between the contract and the actual job, withheld wages, excessive working hours, passport confiscation, abuse, and difficulty getting legal aid; women domestic workers are at particular risk, with past allegations of physical and sexual abuse. He says the problems often begin in Bangladesh, not in Saudi Arabia.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: The columnist says Bangladesh must stop excessive recruitment fees and false promises, hold recruiting agencies accountable, and make digital verification of the contract, salary, working hours, employer and accommodation compulsory before departure; a worker's protection must be secured before leaving the country, not after arrival.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

facts.statement: The columnist proposes that Bangladesh seek from Saudi Arabia: (1) a separate worker protection protocol with measurable commitments (time limit to settle withheld-wage complaints, how a worker can change jobs if the employer breaks the contract, action on passport confiscation, shelter after abuse complaints, who gives legal aid, quick compensation for families of dead or seriously injured workers); (2) lower recruitment cost through a transparent, digital, verifiable recruitment system; (3) joint verification that the salary and job on the visa are what the worker actually gets, via a national digital contract registry linked to the Saudi authorities; (4) more consular and labour wing capacity (complaints, legal aid, mediation with employers, labour court support, emergency shelter) and a secure digital profile for each worker; (5) yearly published indicators such as wages withheld, complaints settled, fraud victims and average recruitment cost.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

key_quote_bn: চাকরি পরিবর্তন ও দেশত্যাগের ক্ষেত্রে নির্দিষ্ট শ্রেণির কর্মীদের স্বাধীনতা বেড়েছে। তবে গৃহকর্মীরা এখনো অনেক ক্ষেত্রে পূর্ণ শ্রম আইনি সুরক্ষার বাইরে।

headline_en: The human trafficking network must be broken
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial after 9 Bangladeshis and one Sudanese died on a rubber boat that left Tobruk, Libya for Greece on 3 August 2026 and drifted to Egypt; 29 more Bangladeshis were rescued and hospitalised in Egypt. It says brokers charge BDT 20-22 lakh for the irregular route to Italy and BDT 12-15 lakh to Greece, cites UNHCR and Frontex figures, and criticises the lack of action against trafficking ringleaders.

facts.statement: On 3 August 2026 a rubber boat with capacity for 25 people left Tobruk, Libya for Greece carrying 42 Bangladeshi and Sudanese nationals; it was meant to reach Greece in 36 hours but ran low on fuel and lost its way, food and water ran out, and in extreme heat 10 people died one by one: 9 Bangladeshis and 1 Sudanese. The bodies were thrown into the sea when they began to decompose.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh embassy in Cairo (confirmation) and survivors' accounts, per the editorial

facts.statement: After the boat from Tobruk landed on the coast of Egypt, the rest were rescued sick and unconscious; 29 Bangladeshis rescued from the boat were being treated at a hospital in Egypt, as confirmed by the Bangladesh embassy in Cairo.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh embassy in Cairo

facts.statement: The August 2026 boat tragedy was the second major accident of 2026 on the irregular sea route from Libya to Europe; earlier, in March 2026, 18 Bangladeshi young men died while going to Italy.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial

facts.statement: According to media reports including Prothom Alo, people have to hand brokers BDT 20 to 22 lakh to go to Italy by the irregular route and BDT 12 to 15 lakh to go to Greece.
facts.source_in_article: media reports including Prothom Alo

facts.statement: An irregular sea route used by Bangladeshis runs from Tobruk in Libya by rubber boat to Greece, a crossing said to take 36 hours; another runs from Libya to Italy across the Mediterranean.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial

facts.statement: UNHCR data: about 11,231 Bangladeshis reached Italy from Libya in the 10 months from January to October 2024.
facts.source_in_article: UNHCR

facts.statement: Frontex data: an estimated 110,000 (1 lakh 10 thousand) Bangladeshis have reached Europe by this risky route since 2009. The editorial says Bangladeshis are ahead of war-torn Afghanistan and Sudan in this risky Mediterranean migration.
facts.source_in_article: Frontex; Prothom Alo editorial

facts.statement: The editorial says that after each major accident one or two local-level brokers are arrested but the ringleaders of trafficking rings stay out of reach; those arrested are hardly ever tried because of weak FIRs and lack of evidence, and Bangladesh lacks the skilled, specialised personnel needed to break the cross-border network. Visible action by the expatriates' welfare ministry and police is absent.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial

key_quote_bn: অবৈধপথে ইতালি যেতে ২০ থেকে ২২ লাখ এবং গ্রিস যেতে ১২ থেকে ১৫ লাখ টাকা দালালদের হাতে তুলে দিতে হচ্ছে।

headline_en: 12 Bangladeshis killed in Middle East war; 4 Bangladeshis killed after going to Russia two and a half months ago
summary_en: In parliament on Thursday 9 July 2026 the expatriates' welfare minister said 12 Bangladeshis had died in the Middle East war and 186 people had been brought home from Iran with Wage Earners' Welfare Board funding. He said 30 workers who went to Russia on 24 April 2026 with BMET manpower clearance were being forcibly prepared for war and four of them were reported dead, and gave an update on Malaysia talks and the number who went to the Middle East since 2004. The rest of the article covers unrelated parliamentary answers on food procurement and disaster losses.

facts.statement: 12 Bangladeshi nationals have died so far in the Middle East war: 5 in Lebanon, 3 in Saudi Arabia, 2 in the United Arab Emirates, and 1 each in Iraq and Bahrain.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, in parliament on 9 July 2026

facts.statement: Of the 12 Bangladeshis killed in the Middle East war, 1 was buried in the country concerned and the bodies of 9 were brought home; their families were given BDT 35,000 at the airport for burial and BDT 50,000 each as a special grant.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, in parliament on 9 July 2026

facts.statement: In the Middle East war situation, 186 people including 12 women and 8 children were brought back to Bangladesh from Iran with Wage Earners' Welfare Board funding.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, in parliament on 9 July 2026

facts.statement: On 24 April 2026, 30 Bangladeshi workers went to Russia with manpower clearance obtained by a recruiting agency from BMET. After arrival, the government received information that they were being forcibly prepared for war and that moves were under way to send them from a camp to the battlefield.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, in parliament on 9 July 2026

facts.statement: Of the 30 Bangladeshi workers who went to Russia on 24 April 2026 with BMET clearance, four have been reported dead according to the latest information.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, in parliament on 9 July 2026

facts.statement: On 15 June 2026 a letter was sent to the Bangladesh embassy in Moscow to take the necessary steps to rescue the endangered Bangladeshi workers and return them home; the government hopes to bring back the remaining workers through contact with the Russian authorities.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, in parliament on 9 July 2026

facts.statement: On sending workers to Malaysia, bilateral talks were held with a high-level Malaysian representative in April 2026, the Prime Minister recently visited Malaysia, and a Malaysian delegation was due to visit Bangladesh in July 2026; the minister hoped the way to send Bangladeshi workers would open very soon (the market was still not open as of 9 July 2026).
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, in parliament on 9 July 2026

facts.statement: According to BMET server data, 10,918,009 (1 crore 9 lakh 18 thousand 9) Bangladeshis went to various Middle Eastern countries for overseas employment from 2004 to 30 June 2026; a large part have returned, and because there is no data on returnees the exact number currently working cannot be given.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, in parliament on 9 July 2026, citing BMET server data
